newsitem.title: USA: U.S. cool to Colombian extradition bill.
newsitem.headline: U.S. cool to Colombian extradition bill.

text.p: The United States on Wednesday withheld judgment on a controversial extradition bill in Colombia but said any such law should have few restrictions and hinted that the proposed measure fell short.
"We need to review the bill very carefully before we can make a full assessment on it," U.S. State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns told reporters.

"But it's our view that any bill that is ultimately enacted must have an absolute minimum of restrictions on extradition to be a truly effective means of cooperation in the fight against narcotics trafficking," he said.

Burns added: "And as you know, we think that we're only going to win the war against drugs in this hemisphere if we have fully effected cooperation from other countries. And that means the ability to extradite a suspect to other countries, in this case, to the United States."

A Colombia Senate panel on Tuesday approved a controversial constitutional reform bill that would partially lift the country's 6-year-old ban on the extradition of drug traffickers and other criminals.
But the bill faces more legislative hurdles before it can become law and was so watered down that some lawmakers said it was essentially useless.

Critics said it opened the door to extradition, if only a crack. But they stressed that it also ruled out the practice in cases where criminals would face stiffer penalties abroad than at home -- or in the case of criminals who give themselves up before they are caught.

The bill would effectively block extradition to the United States, where jail sentences can be much stiffer. Washington has been pressing Colombia to reinstate extradition and cooperate more seriously in the war against drug traffickers.

Asked if the proposed bill would meet U.S. requirements, Burns said: "We need to look at the bill carefully and then we'll make a judgment on it. But we do want the bill to meet a standard that would actually help us fight the war on drugs and to make sure that the narcotraffickers don't have a place to hide."

"They've had lots of places to hide in Colombia, unfortunately, in the last couple of years, and we would like the Colombian government, in this bill, to close off those opportunities of refuge for narcotraffickers. That's the standard that has to be met here," he said.
